WITH tc AS (SELECT CAST(substr(week_of,1,4) AS INT) yr, employee_id, SUM(regular_hours+overtime_hours) paid, COUNT(*) wks FROM hr_timecards GROUP BY 1,2),
lb AS (SELECT CAST(substr(work_date,1,4) AS INT) yr, employee_id, SUM(hours) clk FROM shop_labour_entries GROUP BY 1,2),
r AS (SELECT e.role, tc.yr, SUM(paid) paid, SUM(COALESCE(clk,0)) clk FROM tc LEFT JOIN lb USING(yr,employee_id) JOIN hr_employees e USING(employee_id) WHERE tc.yr BETWEEN 2016 AND 2025 GROUP BY 1,2),
rate AS (SELECT employee_id, arg_max(hourly, effective_on) hourly FROM hr_pay_rates WHERE effective_on <= '2025-12-31' GROUP BY 1),
rr AS (SELECT e.role, median(rate.hourly) med_rate FROM rate JOIN hr_employees e USING(employee_id) WHERE employee_id IN (SELECT employee_id FROM tc WHERE yr=2025) GROUP BY 1),
x AS (SELECT role,
 (SUM(CASE WHEN yr BETWEEN 2023 AND 2025 THEN paid-clk END)-SUM(CASE WHEN yr BETWEEN 2017 AND 2019 THEN paid-clk END))/3.0 d3avg,
 SUM(CASE WHEN yr=2025 THEN paid-clk END)-SUM(CASE WHEN yr=2017 THEN paid-clk END) d17
 FROM r GROUP BY 1)
SELECT role, ROUND(d3avg,0) d3avg, ROUND(d3avg*med_rate,0) usd3avg, ROUND(d17*med_rate,0) usd17,
 ROUND(SUM(d3avg) OVER(),0) t3, ROUND(SUM(d3avg*med_rate) OVER(),0) tusd3, ROUND(SUM(d17*med_rate) OVER(),0) tusd17,
 ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN role IN ('machinist mill','machinist lathe') THEN d3avg*med_rate END) OVER(),0) usd3_machining
FROM x JOIN rr USING(role) ORDER BY role

content.text:
I've revised and saved F9 as `finding.json`. I accepted the challenge in full. I found nothing in it to argue against with new evidence, and the narrower finding is better supported.

**What changed:**
- **Baseline year.** 2016 doesn't work as a starting point. During 2016, hours clocked per estimated hour fell from about 1.0 to about 0.81–0.88, on the same parts with unchanged estimates (q374, q389). That one-off step accounts for 58.5% of the fall in clocked hours from 2016 to 2025 (q385, q391). Measured from 2017, the fall is almost all lower workload: −14,314 h from less work, against +2,342 h from more hours clocked per estimated hour (q385).
- **The 2016 step itself.** The records can't tell whether it was real efficiency or labour no longer being booked to jobs. It is now a question to ask the plant, not something counted as idle capacity.
- **Size.** It drops from $405,555 to **$255,110 a year**, comparing the 2017–19 and 2023–25 averages. I re-ran the pricing myself as q395. The single-year 2017 baseline gives $349,162 (q379), which I keep as an upper reference.
- **What the money means.** It is the value of hours that were already paid, not a cost that grew: total paid hours changed by only +511.3 h from 2016 to 2025 (q391). It comes to 7.92 full-time equivalents spread over 8 roles, with no role above 1.73 (q390).
- **Laser and paint.** Painters drop out as a "staffing added" case: from 2017 their paid hours rose only 213 h (q390). Laser stays in: its workload fell while paid hours rose 1,896 h, partly through deliberate backlog hiring (q386).

**What still stands:**
- **Machining.** Mill and lathe workload fell while their paid hours were held or added. That pattern holds with any baseline and accounts for $116,772 of the $255,110 (q395).
- **Not about individuals.** The rise moves whole roles, not a few employees (q349).
- **No cross-booking.** Every role books 100% of its labour to its own work centre, so the gap isn't hiding at another work centre (q382).

`accepted` is set to true. Confidence stays medium.
